newsitem.title: FRANCE: Search for solo Canadian sailor gathers momentum.
newsitem.headline: Search for solo Canadian sailor gathers momentum.

text.p: Competitors in a round-the-world sailing race are closing in on a remote Antarctic area where third yachtsman was feared in trouble after the dramatic rescue of two colleagues, race organisers said on Thursday.

The organisers' concern for Canadian Gerry Roufs, who has been out of touch since Tuesday night, was mixed with elation over the Australian navy's spectacular rescue of a French and a British competitor.

French yachtswoman Isabelle Autissier has turned back, sailing against high winds towards the area where Roufs could have drifted. She telexed the Paris headquarters of the Vendee Globe race that she expected to reach the area at first light Friday (Thursday afternoon GMT).
Three other competitors, further away but sailing downwind, were also re-routed towards the area, as well as the Panamanian freighter Mas Enterprise,which was 240 miles away on Wednesday night.

There were cheers and shouts of joy at the Paris headquarters early on Thursday when chief organiser Philippe Jeantot was told by telephone that two competitors were rescued more than 2,500 km (1,500 miles) from the Australian coast.
Frenchman Thierry Dubois was plucked from a life raft by helicopter and hours later British solo sailor Tony Bullimore swam into the arms of rescuers after five days beneath his upturned yacht.
The French Foreign Ministry has expressed gratitude to Australian authorities.
Autissier also owes her life to the Australian navy who plucked her from her capsized boat in a 1994 round-the-world solo race in a million-dollar rescue operation.

Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said Australia was not tallying the cost of the rescue missions, but Sport Minister Warwick Smith has written to French counterpart Guy Drut to say the race, one of the world's most dangerous sports events, should be moved to a more northerly and safer route.
Roufs, who was way ahead of the two rescued sailors, was sailing in "the big hole" -- the area between New Zealand and Cape Horn which has no country to its immediate north.

Chile and Argentina were the nearest countries which could be involved in a possible rescue attempt, but search operations were currently coordinated from western France by the French rescue service Cross-Etel.
Organisers said the search covered a cone-shaped area 150 nautical miles long and 80 miles wide.
They said contact had been lost with Roufs' satellite beacon, but the sailor had not set off his alarm signals.

This could mean that his beacon was faulty and Roufs was sailing normally and had deemed it unnecessary to call for help. Or it could indicate he had suffered a serious accident and was unable to call for help.
